title: I feel like I'm the only one trying in my relationship
summary: Feeling like you're the only one trying in your relationship? What's usually underneath the imbalance, and how to tell if it can actually change.
body_text: You made the reservation. You started the hard conversation. You noticed they seemed off, asked about it, and then carried the answer around for the rest of the week. And at some point a thought shows up and will not leave: if I stopped doing all of this, would anything happen at all? The honest answer up front: that feeling points to two very different situations, and they usually get treated as one. Sometimes your partner is putting in real effort that you are not counting, because it does not look like effort to you. Sometimes you really are the only one holding the relationship up. Most advice on this picks a side. It is worth finding out which one you are in before you decide anything. Two situations that feel identical from the inside The first is a mismatch of currency. One person shows love by planning, initiating, talking things through, repairing after a fight. The other shows it by fixing the car, taking the early shift, handling the thing nobody else wanted to handle. Both are trying. Neither feels chosen, because each is being paid in a currency they do not value, and effort that goes unnoticed quietly stops. The second is a real imbalance. One person is running the relationship: the check-ins, the calendar, the repair work, the invisible planning and remembering . The other is a passenger. Not unkind, not hostile, just not steering. This one does not get solved by more appreciation. It gets solved by the passenger deciding to drive, or by you deciding what you can live with. A quick way to feel the difference. In the first, you feel unseen. In the second, you feel alone. The part people leave out when they tell us this In Maia conversations, this usually arrives as a list. The trip I planned. The counselor I found. The three separate times I brought it up. The list is almost always accurate. What tends to surface a few minutes later is something the person did not plan to say: they stopped asking a while ago. Not out loud, anyway. They started running a quiet experiment instead. I will stop reaching out and see if they notice. I will leave it and see how long the dishes sit there. It makes sense. Asking stopped working, so waiting to be chosen feels safer than asking again and getting the same nothing back. But the test has a flaw built into it. Your partner does not know they are being tested. They are failing a class nobody told them they were enrolled in, and every day they fail it, your certainty that they do not care gets a little more solid. By the time it finally comes out, it does not come out as a request. It comes out as a verdict. Why trying harder usually backfires The instinct here is to increase your output. Plan the better weekend. Write the more careful message. Be so obviously good to them that they cannot help but match it. It rarely works, for a plain reason. The more competently you run the relationship, the less any of it requires them. Effort that is never missed is never noticed. Meanwhile the resentment does not sit still while you wait. It leaks out sideways, usually as an edge in your voice over something small, which hands your partner a concrete thing to react to instead of the real problem. Now you are having a fight about your tone. Scorekeeping is the other trap. Once you are counting, you are collecting evidence, and evidence is for a case. Partners can feel when they are being prosecuted, often before the charge is named, and people who feel accused defend themselves rather than step up. How to find out which one you are in Stop testing and run something clearer instead. Two things, in this order. Say the whole thing once, plainly. Not the list. The feeling underneath the list, plus one specific ask. Something like: "I feel like I am carrying us right now, and I am tired, and I do not want to be the only one who notices when we are drifting. Can you plan one thing for the two of us this month, start to finish, without me involved?" It is small on purpose. Small asks are legible. "Try harder" is not. Then leave real space, and do not fill it. This is the hard half. If you ask them to handle something and then handle it yourself on day three because it was not moving fast enough, you have answered your own question and learned nothing. Let it be a little worse for a while. That gap is the only place their effort has room to show up. What you are watching for is not a perfect performance. It is movement. Did they do it, or something in the neighborhood of it? Did they come back to the conversation on their own without you reopening it? When they said sorry, did anything actually change after? One real attempt, even a clumsy one, tells you more than a month of good intentions. If nothing moves Give it a few weeks, not a few days. But if you have said it clearly, made a specific and small ask, left the space, and the answer is still nothing, then you have your information. The problem at that point is not that they do not understand you. It is that they are not willing, and no better phrasing fixes willingness. That is worth saying without softening it, because people in this spot tend to keep upgrading their technique for years. You can love someone who is not going to meet you. What you do with that is a separate question, and a fair one to sit with slowly: whether this is a rough patch or something you should stop trying to fix , and how much of yourself has already gone into holding it together . One thing worth separating out. If any of this involves fear, or being punished for asking, that is a different situation than an unequal relationship, and it is worth talking to someone you trust or the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233, US). If you are somewhere in the middle of this and genuinely cannot tell whether you are unseen or actually alone, that is a good thing to talk through out loud with the real details in it: what you have asked for, what you quietly stopped asking for, and what you would need to see to feel differently. Maia can help you work out which of these you are in, and what to say next.

title: How AfterQuery Helped NVIDIA Hill-Climb GDPval
summary: AfterQuery is an applied research lab curating data solutions to accelerate foundation model development.
body_text: NVIDIA publicly used AfterQuery’s Off-The-Shelf Office Agent Training Dataset to improve Nemotron 3 Ultra on GDPval . Nemotron 3 Ultra is a fully open 550B-A55B LatentMoE model with open weights, training data, and recipes. Ultra runs at up to ~6× the throughput of comparable open models (5.9× vs GLM-5.1, 4.8× vs Kimi K2.6) on long-horizon agentic tasks at the same accuracy, and supports a context length of up to 1M tokens. AfterQuery is the only data partner named in the Nemotron 3 Ultra technical report : “We then constructed a training distribution from AfterQuery (AQ) tasks that share important latent structure with GDPval, including file-grounded reasoning, professional deliverables, multi-step analysis, and judged final outputs. For each AQ task, we used a strong model to generate multiple full trajectory rollouts. These rollouts were used in two stages. First, before pivot RL, we performed light SFT directly on the student Ultra model. The goal of this step was to transfer the strong model’s workflow priors for GDPval-like tasks to the student. Second, after this MOPD warmup, we proceeded with pivot RL in the MOPD stage, distilling the SFT-trained teacher into the student Ultra model using pivots derived from the strong model’s AQ rollouts.” What is GDPval GDPval is OpenAI’s benchmark for real-world professional tasks. It spans 44 occupations across the nine largest sectors of US GDP, with 1,320 tasks (220 of them open-sourced) drawn from the real work of industry professionals who average 14 years of experience. Each task gives the model a prompt, often with reference files, and asks for a finished deliverable: a spreadsheet, slide deck, document, diagram, etc. Artificial Analysis maintains a public leaderboard version, GDPval-AA v2 , that scores models on the open tasks and is now the highest-weighted evaluation in their Intelligence Index. Models solve the tasks agentically, working in a sandbox with shell + web access via the Stirrup harness. The resulting deliverables are compared in blind pairwise matchups, each graded by a judge sampled from a rotating panel of three frontier LLMs, and those results are fit to an Elo scale anchored to human expert work at 1,000 Elo. AfterQuery’s Office Agent tasks mirror GDPval task structure, with file-grounded inputs, multi-step analysis, and rubrics. PivotRL PivotRL (Yi et al., 2026) is a turn-level RL method for agent training. It starts from existing SFT trajectories and treats each assistant turn as a possible training state. For each candidate turn, it samples several next actions from the reference or initial policy and scores them with a verifier. It keeps only the turns where the sampled actions produce mixed outcomes—some pass, some fail—and discards turns that are already uniformly solved or uniformly failed. RL is then run locally at those retained “pivot” turns, using verifier rewards for functionally valid actions rather than exact matches to the demonstration. The intended benefit is lower rollout cost: on SWE-Bench, the paper reports accuracy comparable to end-to-end RL with about 4× fewer rollout turns. Impact The practical use case for PivotRL shows up in NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra training recipe. For GDPval-like office tasks, NVIDIA first used a strong model to generate full AfterQuery trajectories, then reused intermediate decision points from those trajectories as pivots during the MOPD stage. In other words: PivotRL supplies the local “where should we train?” states, while MOPD (Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation) supplies the teacher-student learning signal at those states. NVIDIA trained specialized teachers by domain and then distilled them into Ultra through MOPD. For the office/workplace teacher, the AfterQuery tasks were chosen because they resemble GDPval: file-grounded reasoning, multi-step analysis, professional deliverables, and judged final outputs. The report says the AQ rollouts were used in two stages: a light SFT warmup to transfer the strong model’s workflow priors, followed by pivot RL in MOPD using pivots from those same strong-model rollouts. Domain Student No warmup Warmup Teacher GDPval 28.9 35.3 46.7 49.5 BrowseComp 31.0 33.0 44.4 51.0 HLE (no tools) 25.6 26.3 26.7 32.1 NVIDIA’s warmup ablation. Student is the starting checkpoint, Teacher the specialized model being distilled toward. On GDPval, warmup raises the MOPD result from 35.3 to 46.7, leaving Ultra only 2.8 points behind the office/workplace teacher. BrowseComp shows the same pattern, rising from 33.0 to 44.4. HLE barely moves, from 26.3 to 26.7. AfterQuery has similarly validated that on-policy distillation works well for improving models on GDPval-style tasks, reaching a +20.9% net win-loss margin over base with a Nemotron 3 Nano student with pure OPD. AfterQuery is an applied research lab curating data solutions to accelerate foundation model development. Sources: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra technical report (Tables 4–5, Office & Workplace Task Teacher); PivotRL, Yi et al., 2026 (arXiv 2603.21383v1); GDPval-AA v2 leaderboard.

title: TotalEnergies, TES, Osaka Gas, Toho Gas and ITOCHU Partner Up to Develop the Live Oak Project for e-NG Production in Nebraska
summary: TotalEnergies, TES, Osaka Gas, Toho Gas, and ITOCHU signed a Joint Development and Operating Agreement giving the Japanese partners a 33.3% stake in Live Oak.
body_text: Download the Press Release Paris, December 2, 2025 – TotalEnergies, TES, Osaka Gas, Toho Gas, and ITOCHU have signed a Joint Development and Operating Agreement, granting the Japanese companies a combined 33.3% stake in the Live Oak project — a large-scale facility to produce electric natural gas (e-NG) also known as e-methane, initiated by TotalEnergies and TES and currently under development in Nebraska, United States. Following the agreement, TotalEnergies and TES will each maintain a 33.35% stake in the project. The partners are now preparing the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) phase, targeting a capacity of approximately 250 MW of electrolysis and 75 ktpa of methanation. The project, subject to a Final Investment Decision in 2027, is scheduled to begin commercial operations by 2030, with plans to export e-NG to Japan. Osaka Gas and Toho Gas will be the primary offtakers. This project helps the Japanese gas majors in achieving their goal of injecting 1% carbon neutral gas (such as e-NG) into the gas grid by 2030. The agreement builds on the strategic partnership established between TotalEnergies and TES in 2023 to pioneer at scale production of e-NG. The Live Oak project will leverage Nebraska’s abundant biogenic CO2 resources, captured from bioethanol plants, and the growing renewable power generation capacity in the United States. The participation of Osaka Gas, Toho Gas, and ITOCHU (as a coordinator of Japanese companies), underscores their commitment to decarbonization with the adoption of e-NG and positions Live Oak as the leading project for carbon-neutral gas production for Japan. e-NG is a synthetic gas produced from renewable hydrogen and CO2. Chemically identical to conventional natural gas, e-NG can be seamlessly integrated into existing LNG infrastructure—liquefaction, transport, regasification, and distribution—without any alterations to consumer equipment. *** About TotalEnergies TotalEnergies is a global integrated energy company that produces and markets energies: oil and biofuels, natural gas, biogas and low-carbon hydrogen, renewables and electricity. Our more than 100,000 employees are committed to provide as many people as possible with energy that is more reliable, more affordable and more sustainable. Active in about 120 countries, TotalEnergies places sustainability at the heart of its strategy, its projects and its operations. About TES TES is a global green energy company developing giga-scale projects to accelerate the energy transition. In Europe, TES’ projects strengthen energy security and the diversification of energy imports, as well as support the European Union’s decarbonisation efforts. In Wilhelmshaven, Germany, TES is developing green energy terminal, that will serve as a major hub for sustainable molecules. The already operating floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) will be followed by a large-scale onshore LNG terminal and a CO2 export terminal. Globally, TES leverages renewable energy solar, wind, and hydro, along with climate-neutral CO2 for the production of e-NG (electric natural gas). Large-scale e-NG projects are underway in the US (Live Oak), Canada (Project Mauricie), and across Europe, and the Middle East. These green molecules support the shift to real zero emissions across industries and help win the race against climate change. About Osaka Gas The Daigas Group is dedicated to realizing a carbon-neutral future through its Carbon Neutral Vision and Energy Transition 2050 initiative. As part of this effort, the Group aims to integrate 1% e-methane into its gas grid by 2030, paving the way for broader adoption across society. To achieve this goal, the Group is actively advancing e-methane technologies, conducting demonstration projects, and building supply chains both in Japan and overseas—driving progress toward carbon neutrality by 2050. About Toho Gas Toho Gas aims to make its entire supply chain including its customers’ sites carbon neutral by 2050. To this end, Toho Gas is currently accelerating initiatives that contribute to the low-carbon transition and further decarbonization of its customers. Toho Gas will devote itself to realizing a decarbonized society and further development of Chubu region by securing and providing diverse and optimal decarbonized energy sources, including e-methane and biogas. About ITOCHU ITOCHU is involved in domestic trading, import/export, and overseas trading of various products, as well as business investment in Japan and overseas. ITOCHU, with the group’s corporate mission “Sampo-yoshi” (good for the seller, good for the buyer and good for society), is pursuing a policy of enhancing its contribution to and engagement with the SDGs through business activities, including promoting e-NG, as a member of the e-NG Coalition. title: How RelaDyne Turned Motor Oil Into a Service Contract
summary: RelaDyne made MDM's 2025 Top Distributors list in Lubricants & Fuels. Its edge isn't the oil in the drum, it's the service wrapped around it.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors lists . RelaDyne shows up on Modern Distribution Management's 2025 Top Distributors list in the Lubricants & Fuels vertical, one of roughly 20 categories MDM uses to rank North America's largest wholesale distributors. The company runs more than 190 locations and was built almost entirely by acquisition. But the interesting part of RelaDyne's story isn't the roll-up math. It's what the company sells alongside the oil, and why that, not the oil itself, is the thing customers can't easily walk away from. Four companies, one merger, no single founder RelaDyne doesn't have a founder-and-garage origin story. It was created in November 2010 when four independent petroleum distributors merged into a single platform, according to the company's own history page : Mid-Town Petroleum of Bridgeview, Illinois; Oil Distributing Company of Cincinnati; The Hurt Company of Houston; and Pumpelly Oil Company of Sulphur, Louisiana. Two of those four, Hurt and Pumpelly, came out of Gulf Coast oil-patch territory, which is part of why RelaDyne still carries real oilfield and energy-sector DNA even though its MDM listing sits under the broader Lubricants & Fuels category rather than a pure-play energy one. That structure, four regional leaders combined at once rather than one company gradually buying out weaker rivals, set the operating pattern RelaDyne has run for sixteen years since: acquire established regional distributors, and keep going. Buying family businesses and keeping their names on the door What stands out in how RelaDyne integrates acquisitions is what it doesn't do: it rarely erases the acquired brand. Seaboard Neumann, now marketed as "a RelaDyne Company," traces back to a 1997 Motorcraft distributorship partnership between Jack Becker Distributors and Flamingo Oil Company. It picked up Coastal Unilube's Central Florida operations in 2003, acquired Neumann Oil Company (in business since 1933) in 2010, and added Clean Diesel Services in 2012, all before RelaDyne folded it into the family. The RelaDyne name sits beside Seaboard Neumann's, not over it. That pattern repeats across the portfolio. Distribution reliability-services brands like Sicelub, Lubritech, COT-Puritech, and Clarus Fluid Intelligence still operate under their own names inside RelaDyne, each with decades of standing in its own regional market. For a company built on serial acquisition, that's a real choice. Most roll-ups rebrand fast to prove the platform is real. RelaDyne has bet the opposite way: that a Neumann Oil customer in Central Florida trusts the Neumann name more than a national one, and that preserving it is worth more than a tidy org chart. The oil gets you in the door. The service is the business. Here's the part of RelaDyne's model that's easy to miss if you only look at the product list. Lubricants and fuel are commodities. Anyone with a tank truck can sell 15W-40 at a competitive price. RelaDyne's reliability-services arm is what turns that transaction into something stickier: in-plant lubrication technicians, oil analysis and condition monitoring, tank cleaning and varnish removal, fueling-management programs, equipment installation and repair. A customer who signs up for RelaDyne's lubrication-management program isn't just buying drums of oil on a schedule. They've handed over a maintenance function. That's the unique insight worth naming plainly: RelaDyne behaves less like an oil company that added services, and more like an industrial-services company that happens to sell oil as the entry ticket. Once a plant's lubrication program, tank monitoring, and technician visits run through RelaDyne, switching suppliers means re-engineering a maintenance process, not just calling a different sales rep for the next order. That is a harder moat to build than volume pricing, and a much harder one for a competitor to dislodge. The growth engine hasn't slowed down RelaDyne's acquisition pace in 2026 alone: Dion and Sons , a Southern California petroleum and industrial-reliability provider, in February, and Chart Distribution Group, a Midwest lubricants and detailing distributor, in June. In 2023, RelaDyne expanded outside the U.S. entirely, adding Grupo Lucalza to extend its footprint into Mexico and Guatemala, a notable move for a distributor whose MDM category peers are almost entirely domestic operators. Year Move 2010 Merger of four founding companies creates RelaDyne 2012 Seaboard Neumann adds Clean Diesel Services 2023 Grupo Lucalza acquisition extends reach into Mexico and Guatemala 2026 Dion and Sons (Feb.) and Chart Distribution Group (June) acquired The company also picked up a 2026 CIO 100 Award for its technology program and named Leigh Dobbs as Chief Human Resources Officer in July 2026, both signals of a platform still investing in the back office rather than coasting on scale. The trade-off nobody puts on the About page Serving a dozen-plus industries, agriculture, aviation, construction, defense and maritime, fleets, manufacturing, mining, nuclear, petrochemical, and power generation, insulates RelaDyne from any single sector's downturn, including the oil-and-gas cycles its Houston and Louisiana founding companies know well. That diversification is a genuine strength. It's also a real cost: a company this spread out doesn't get to be the obvious answer for any one buyer the way a specialist competitor can. RelaDyne isn't the oilfield lubricants company or the fleet-fluids company. It's the reliability-services company that happens to serve all of them, which is a harder story to tell in a single sales pitch but a much steadier one to run a business on. Distribution excellence rarely looks like the product on the label. More often it's the tank gauge, the technician on-site, and the maintenance schedule nobody outside the plant ever sees.

title: How digital skills wallets help learners showcase skills beyond the transcript
summary: How digital skills wallets help learners showcase skills beyond the transcript | Pearson plc
body_text: Workforce & Skills July 27, 2026 Carie Addis SHARE Share this item with Copy this link https://plc.pearson.com/en-GB/news-and-insights/blogs/how-digital-skills-wallets-help-learners-showcase-skills-beyond-transcript Key takeaways Traditional transcripts capture academic performance but often miss skills, experiences and achievements developed beyond the classroom. Digital skills wallets help learners build a richer record of their learning journey. Learning and Employment Records (LERs) can help institutions better demonstrate learner outcomes and support transitions into further study and work. Carie Addis, Head of Strategic Partnerships, Pearson What’s missing from a traditional transcript? Every educator can picture one: the natural leader whose transcript happens to show a B in history. The learner who builds remarkable things in robotics club but has no official record of technical skills. The graduate who carried a real-world project from start to finish, but whose resume can’t fully capture that blend of collaboration and analysis. You see the potential. You know what they can do. The problem is that the document handed to learners at graduation — the transcript, the diploma — flattens all of it into a narrow snapshot. For a long time, everyone downstream accepted the snapshot as shorthand. That acceptance is starting to change. Why the snapshot stopped being enough Two things changed at once. Hiring shifted toward demonstrated skills. Employers increasingly want to know what a candidate can do and a course title alone doesn’t answer that question. At the same time, AI made it easier to generate a polished resume and faked credentials. When claims become easier to make, actual evidence becomes more valuable. For institutions, that creates a new challenge. The question is no longer whether learning happened—it’s whether your graduates can prove it, instantly, to anyone who asks. What is a digital skills wallet? A digital skills wallet is designed to help learners do exactly that. It’s a secure, learner-owned record that holds degrees, certifications, project work, and applied skills in one place — while giving learners control over how those achievements are shared. For a graduate, that might mean sharing proof of technical skills with a tech recruiter, a project management certification with a hiring manager, and a degree with a graduate school — each in a single, secure action, each independently verifiable. No transcript request, no waiting, no doubt about authenticity. For institutions, it changes what a credential can represent. Instead of a grid of grades, your students leave holding a rich, verified record of what they have achieved, demonstrated and developed over time. How do digital wallets benefit educational institutions? The benefits extend beyond the individual learner. Less friction at every handoff. Applications, transfers and workforce entry are still often slow and manual, built on records that are hard to verify. A portable, verified record removes helps simplify those transactions. Clearer proof of learner outcome. When achievements can be linked to verified skills and experiences rather than course completions, you can see them — which programs produce which capabilities, where the gaps are, how investment maps to real student progress. Learners who compete on proof. As hiring tilts toward validated skills, the institutions whose students can demonstrate capability hold a real advantage. The credential becomes something a learner can put to work immediately – a clear signal of its value. How Pearson supports learner records at scale Making this real takes more than a wallet app. It takes trusted credentials, open standards, and the scale to be recognized everywhere a learner goes. Pearson brings those elements together through its credentialling ecosystem. Through Credly, Pearson has issued over 100 million verified digital credentials, helping learners capture and share achievements across education, professional learning, and workforce development. Built on open standards — including W3C Verifiable Credentials and Open Badges 3.0 — so they move with the learner rather than staying locked to a single system. For institutions, that means the shift to a portable, verified record isn’t a leap into the unknown. It’s building on a standard that already works. From transcript to lifelong learning record The traditional transcript served its purpose in a world where a snapshot of achievement was enough. Learners today — and the employers waiting for them — need something that reflects how people learn, develop skills, and grow throughout their life. A learner’s story doesn’t begin with a diploma and end with a first job. It continues through higher education, professional development, and lifelong learning. The records that support that journey should evolve as well. The institutions shifting to this now won’t just be keeping pace. They’ll be the ones whose learners can prove their worth the instant they’re asked. To see how Pearson is advancing digital skills wallets, verified credentials, and Learning and Employment Records, visit plc.pearson.com . Email alerts Press contacts

title: IVA en Colombia: tarifas, períodos y cómo declararlo
summary: El IVA (Impuesto sobre las Ventas) en Colombia tiene tres tarifas vigentes en 2026: 19% general, 5% reducida para un grupo específico de bienes y servicios, y 0% para los llamados bienes exentos y excluidos.
body_text: El IVA (Impuesto sobre las Ventas) en Colombia tiene tres tarifas vigentes en 2026: 19% general , 5% reducida para un grupo específico de bienes y servicios, y 0% para los llamados bienes exentos y excluidos. Si eres responsable de este impuesto, debes declararlo de forma bimestral, cuatrimestral o anual según tus ingresos, usando el Formulario 300 a través del portal de la DIAN. A continuación te explicamos qué tarifa aplica a cada caso, cada cuánto se declara y el paso a paso para presentar la declaración sin errores. Las 3 (realmente 4) tarifas de IVA vigentes en 2026 Aunque se habla de "tres tarifas", en la práctica existen cuatro tratamientos distintos porque el 0% se divide en dos categorías con reglas diferentes: Tarifa A quién aplica Ejemplos comunes 19% (general) Todo bien o servicio que no esté clasificado expresamente en otra categoría Electrodomésticos, ropa, calzado, vehículos, gaseosas, servicios de telefonía e internet residencial de estratos 4, 5 y 6, licores, cigarrillos, servicios digitales del exterior (streaming, apps, marketplaces) 5% (reducida) Bienes y servicios listados en el artículo 468-1 del Estatuto Tributario Café tostado, embutidos, algunos seguros, cierta maquinaria agrícola 0% – Exentos Bienes gravados a tarifa cero; el productor sí puede descontar el IVA pagado en insumos y pedir devolución Carnes, leche, huevos, queso, arroz, exportaciones 0% – Excluidos Bienes que no causan IVA en ningún caso; el vendedor NO puede descontar el IVA de sus compras Educación (preescolar a universitaria), la mayoría de la canasta básica familiar, algunos servicios de salud Exento vs. excluido: la diferencia que más confunde Para el comprador, exento y excluido se sienten igual: no paga IVA . Pero para el vendedor, la diferencia es fundamental: Bien exento: sí es una operación gravada, solo que a tarifa 0%. El vendedor puede tomar como descontable el IVA que pagó en sus compras relacionadas con ese bien y, en ciertos casos, solicitar la devolución de ese saldo a favor ante la DIAN. Bien excluido: no es una operación gravada en absoluto. El vendedor no genera IVA en la venta, pero tampoco puede descontar el IVA que pagó en sus insumos; ese IVA se convierte en un mayor costo de su operación. Confundir ambas categorías es uno de los errores más comunes al momento de calcular el IVA descontable y puede llevar a solicitar devoluciones improcedentes ante la DIAN. Cada cuánto se declara el IVA: períodos en 2026 La periodicidad depende de tus ingresos brutos del año gravable anterior (2025) y de tu tipo de contribuyente: Periodicidad Quién la usa Tope de ingresos brutos (año anterior) Meses de declaración en 2026 Bimestral Grandes Contribuyentes, responsables de bienes exentos/exportadores (Arts. 477 y 481 ET), y quienes superen el tope de ingresos Igual o superior a 92.000 UVT (aprox. $4.581.508.000) Marzo, mayo, julio, septiembre, noviembre y enero 2027 Cuatrimestral La mayoría de responsables del régimen ordinario Inferior a 92.000 UVT Mayo, septiembre y enero 2027 Anual Contribuyentes del Régimen Simple de Tributación (RST) que son responsables de IVA No aplica; depende de pertenecer al RST Declaración anual, con anticipos bimestrales durante el año Si tu negocio apenas inicia operaciones y no tienes ingresos del año anterior con qué comparar, la DIAN te asigna automáticamente periodicidad bimestral durante tu primer año. Cómo declarar el IVA paso a paso Presentar el Formulario 300 no es complicado si sigues el orden correcto: Verifica tu responsabilidad en el RUT. Asegúrate de que tengas activo el código 48 (Impuesto sobre las ventas – IVA) y confirma tu periodicidad. Reúne tu información contable del período. Necesitas el total de ventas gravadas, exentas y excluidas, el IVA generado en tus ventas, y el IVA descontable de tus compras y gastos relacionados con tu actividad. Concilia con tu facturación electrónica. Compara tus registros contables contra el reporte de documentos electrónicos emitidos y recibidos en el sistema de la DIAN; cualquier diferencia debe explicarse antes de declarar. Ingresa al portal Transaccional de la DIAN con tu usuario y contraseña (o firma electrónica, según el caso). Usa la Declaración Sugerida de IVA , si está disponible para tu NIT. La DIAN prellena buena parte del formulario con la información que ya tiene de tu facturación electrónica; tú debes revisarla y ajustarla, no darla por hecha automáticamente. Diligencia el Formulario 300 , distribuyendo los valores en sus secciones de ingresos (casillas de ventas gravadas, exentas y excluidas), IVA generado, IVA descontable y liquidación privada. Verifica el saldo resultante: si el IVA generado es mayor al descontable, tendrás un saldo a pagar; si es al contrario, tendrás un saldo a favor que puedes solicitar en devolución o compensar en períodos futuros. Presenta y paga dentro del plazo que te corresponde según el último dígito de tu NIT, consultando el calendario tributario vigente. Guarda el soporte de presentación y pago como respaldo ante cualquier requerimiento posterior de la DIAN. Qué pasa si declaras tarde, no declaras o te equivocas Extemporaneidad: por presentar la declaración después del plazo, la sanción parte del 5% del impuesto a cargo por cada mes o fracción de mes de retraso. Sanción mínima: aplica incluso si no tenías impuesto a pagar en el período; para 2026 equivale a 10 UVT, es decir, cerca de $524.000. No declarar: si la DIAN debe liquidar el impuesto de oficio porque nunca presentaste la declaración, la sanción es considerablemente más alta que la de extemporaneidad y se suma a intereses moratorios. Errores o inconsistencias: declarar valores incorrectos (por ejemplo, tomar como descontable un IVA que no correspondía) puede generar sanción por inexactitud, además de que la DIAN puede rechazar el saldo a favor mal calculado. En cualquiera de estos escenarios, corregir voluntariamente antes de que la DIAN te requiera suele salir más económico que esperar a una fiscalización. Devolución del saldo a favor de IVA Si tu IVA descontable supera al generado, no siempre puedes pedir la devolución en efectivo; este beneficio está limitado principalmente a: Productores de bienes exentos (Art. 477 del ET), como los del sector agropecuario. Contribuyentes que sufrieron retenciones de IVA que generaron un exceso de saldo a favor. Casos especiales, como constructores de vivienda de interés social (VIS). Si no calificas para devolución, generalmente puedes arrastrar el saldo a favor y compensarlo contra el IVA generado en los períodos siguientes. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Los restaurantes cobran IVA o impuesto al consumo? Depende del tipo de establecimiento y si opera bajo franquicia. En general, los restaurantes cobran el Impuesto Nacional al Consumo (INC) del 8%, no IVA, salvo excepciones puntuales. Confundir ambos impuestos es un error frecuente al hacer cálculos. ¿Los servicios digitales del exterior (streaming, apps) pagan IVA en Colombia? Sí, desde 2018 los proveedores de servicios digitales desde el exterior deben cobrar IVA del 19% a los usuarios en Colombia, bajo un régimen especial de recaudo. ¿Si tengo saldo a favor, puedo dejar de presentar la declaración? No. Estar inscrito como responsable te obliga a presentar la declaración en cada período, tengas o no impuesto a pagar, salvo las excepciones puntuales que aplican cuando no hubo ningún tipo de operación en el período. ¿Qué pasa si mi proveedor me cobra una tarifa de IVA que no corresponde? Puedes solicitarle la corrección de la factura. Tomar un IVA descontable con una tarifa incorrecta puede generarte inconsistencias frente a la DIAN al momento de declarar. ¿La Declaración Sugerida de la DIAN reemplaza a mi contador? No. Es una ayuda que prellena información a partir de tus documentos electrónicos, pero la responsabilidad de verificar que los valores sean correctos sigue siendo tuya (o de tu contador).

title: Your LinkedIn Photo Is Costing You Recruiter Replies (and When to Remove It Entirely)
summary: Your LinkedIn photo is the first thing a recruiter sees. Here's the headshot that lifts replies, the mistakes that quietly cost you, and when to remove it.
body_text: Is your LinkedIn photo costing you recruiter replies? It can be, and it's one of the fastest things to fix. A photo is usually the first thing a recruiter sees on your profile, and a missing or bad one reads as an incomplete or abandoned account. A clear, well-lit shot of your face lifts profile views and messages noticeably. You don't need a photographer to get one. And whether to have a photo at all is a real judgment call, because a photo also reveals your age and appearance, which is a genuine trade-off worth thinking about. Here's a fix that takes ten minutes and almost nobody prioritizes. Your LinkedIn photo. Not your headline, not your About section, not the twelfth bullet on your last role. The little circle in the top-left of your profile that a recruiter's eye lands on before they've read a single word. Most job seekers treat it as an afterthought, which is exactly why fixing it pays off so cheaply. People pour hours into the wording of their profile and then leave up a cropped wedding photo, or a blank grey silhouette, or a selfie taken in a car with the seatbelt visible. The words might be great. The first impression already happened before anyone got to them. So let's talk about what a good LinkedIn photo actually is, the quiet mistakes that cost you replies, how to shoot a decent one with a phone, and the honest question of whether you should have a photo up at all. Why the photo matters more than people think Start with the sequence of a recruiter's day. They run a search, get back a wall of small circular thumbnails and names, and start scanning. The photo loads before the text does. It's the first signal, and on LinkedIn, unlike almost anywhere else in a job search, that signal is a picture of your face. People in executive search put it simply: a profile isn't a resume. A resume is a document of record, and it can be a little dry and still do its job. A profile has a different job. Its whole point is to make a stranger feel like there's a specific, real person on the other end, someone they might want to message, refer, or interview. That framing matters, because how recruiters actually use LinkedIn is far more about scanning for a real, contactable human than most job seekers assume. A face does that. It's the difference between a business card and a handshake. There's also a trust dimension that has gotten sharper lately. Fake profiles are a real thing, bots are everywhere, and a blank or generic avatar now reads as slightly suspicious to a recruiter who scans hundreds of profiles a week. It's a small piece of a much larger machine, and it helps to know how hiring actually works end to end, because the profile photo sits right at the top of the funnel where a recruiter first decides whether to look closer. A missing photo doesn't come across as private or modest. It comes across as incomplete, or abandoned, or possibly not a real account at all. When someone has a second and a half to decide if you're worth a message, "I can't even see who this is" is not a great place to start. On the numbers, LinkedIn has long claimed that profiles with a photo get dramatically more views and messages than profiles without one. Those specific multipliers get quoted everywhere, but they trace back to old LinkedIn-attributed figures that are hard to verify against a current source, so treat them as folklore rather than fact. The direction, though, is consistent across everything recruiters actually say: a clear photo gets you noticed more and replied to more. You don't need the exact multiplier to act on that. What a good headshot actually is Strip away the marketing and a good LinkedIn photo comes down to a handful of things any recruiter would recognize. Your face fills most of the frame. This is the big one and the most commonly botched. Crop so your head and the top of your shoulders take up the majority of the square. A useful rule of thumb people in the business toss around is that your face should occupy at least around 60% of the photo. If someone has to squint to find you in the picture, the picture isn't working. Thumbnail-first means the details that look fine on a full screen vanish at the size a recruiter actually sees. It's well lit and your face is clear. Soft, even light on your face, no harsh shadow cutting across it, and enough resolution that you don't go pixelated when someone clicks in. Clarity does more work than any styling trick. If your face reads clearly and looks friendly, you're most of the way there. You look approachable. A real, slight smile beats a stern corporate stare, and it beats a full toothy grin that looks staged. Eye contact with the camera matters more than people expect, because it's what makes the photo feel like the person is looking at you. The read you want is "someone I'd be glad to get on a call with," not "someone posing for a passport." The background is simple and quiet. A plain wall, a clean office, some soft outdoor blur. Anything that doesn't pull the eye off your face. A busy or distracting background makes the whole thing read as casual, and casual is the wrong register for the one photo a hiring manager is judging. You're dressed about one notch above the room. Match the norm of the job you want and then step it up a small amount. For most office and corporate roles that means a collared shirt or a simple top in a solid color. For a creative or startup role you can be more relaxed. The goal isn't a suit for its own sake, it's looking like you'd fit in on a good day at that workplace. It's recent, and it's you alone. The photo should look like the person who'll walk into the interview or show up on the video call. And it should be just you, no cropped-out friend's shoulder, no second face, no arm around someone. One person, your actual current face, clear enough to recognize. Notice what's not on that list: expensive, professionally shot, retouched. None of that is required. A normal, clean photo of a real person who looks approachable clears the bar. Plenty of well-regarded people on the platform have perfectly ordinary, non-studio photos, and they do fine. The quiet mistakes that cost you replies Most bad LinkedIn photos aren't offensively bad. They're just a little off in a way that quietly lowers how seriously you get taken. Here are the ones recruiters flag most, each with the quick fix. The cropped group or wedding photo. You looked great at the wedding, so you cut yourself out of it. Now there's a disembodied arm on your shoulder, or half of someone else's face, or a strand of hair the crop couldn't kill. Fix: take a solo photo. It's ten minutes and it's the single highest-return swap on this list. Sunglasses or a hat. Anything covering your eyes defeats the entire purpose. People trust faces they can see, and eye contact is doing a lot of the work. Fix: no sunglasses, no brim shadowing your face. Let people see your eyes. The distant full-body or podium shot. A photo of you at a lectern from thirty feet away, or a full-length shot where your face is a tiny smudge. It looks impressive on a big screen and disappears in a thumbnail. Fix: crop tight to chest-up, or reshoot. If they have to zoom to find your face, it's too far away. The car or bathroom selfie. Recruiters call these out by name, because they show up constantly. A seatbelt across your chest or a bathroom mirror behind you tells a hiring manager you spent zero effort on the one image they're evaluating. Fix: stand against a plain wall near a window and have someone take it. Same phone, completely different impression. Heavy filters or a party backdrop. The beauty filter that smooths you into someone else, the neon Vegas sign behind your head, the drink in your hand. LinkedIn is a professional room, and a photo that looks like a night out makes a reader wonder why it's there at all. Fix: neutral setting, natural look, save the fun photos for elsewhere. A logo, cartoon, or avatar instead of a face. A company logo, an anime-style illustration, a Bitmoji, a stock silhouette. These are among the most disliked choices recruiters mention, because the whole value of the photo is a real human face building a little trust. A logo builds none of that. Fix: use an actual photo of yourself. If you genuinely can't, a blank default is honestly better than a cartoon. The stiff, decade-old badge photo. The formal corporate portrait from three jobs ago where you look like you're being processed rather than met. Or worse, a much younger version of you that you quietly reverted to. It creates a small recognizability gap the moment you meet someone in person, and reverting to a younger photo tends to read as exactly the insecurity it's trying to hide. Fix: a current, relaxed photo that looks like you today. Low light and hard shadows. Shot indoors under a ceiling light so half your face is dark, or in direct noon sun so you're squinting with a shadow slashing across your nose. Fix: shoot in open shade on a sunny day, or on an overcast day, where the light wraps softly around your face with no harsh edges. Not sure how your profile reads to a recruiter? Get a free LinkedIn review that checks your photo, headline, and profile against what recruiters actually screen for. Review My LinkedIn → You don't need a pro (the ten-minute DIY recipe) The good news buried under all the AI-headshot ads is that a phone gets you most of the way there. Here's the recipe, and it really is this simple. Find soft, even light. The easiest source is a window. Stand facing it, a few feet back, so the daylight lands flat on your face. Outdoors, don't shoot in direct sun. Stand in open shade on a bright day, or wait for an overcast sky, so the light is even and there are no hard shadows. A plain wall behind you works fine, and a brick wall in shade looks genuinely good. Put on a solid-color top. A collared shirt, a plain blouse, a crewneck sweater, whatever fits the job you want, just nothing with a loud pattern that fights your face for attention. Then hand the phone to a friend instead of shooting a selfie. A photo taken from a couple of feet away at eye level looks far more natural than an arm's-length front camera, which distorts your nose and flattens everything else. Frame it from about the second or third button of your shirt up to just above your head. Portrait mode helps if your phone has it, since it softly blurs the background. Take twenty shots, not one. Have your friend crack a joke between frames so the smile is real and not the frozen one you make when someone says "smile." Then pick the frame where you look like a person you'd actually want to work with, and delete the other nineteen. If the background still looks messy, there are free tools that remove it cleanly and let you drop in a plain color, and a few dollars on a photo-editing community gets you a professional-looking backdrop swap. That's the whole thing. Ten minutes, no studio, no invoice. It clears the bar that matters, which is a clear, well-lit, friendly face. What about those AI headshot generators? You've seen the ads. Upload a dozen selfies, pay around twenty dollars, and get back a couple hundred polished corporate headshots in a studio you never visited. As a category they're a reasonable option for someone who wants a clean result fast and doesn't have a decent photo to start from. There's one caveat worth taking seriously, and it comes from the people who actually shoot portraits for a living. AI results can land in an uncanny zone. Something's subtly off, the skin a touch too plasticky, the eyes not quite tracking, and a sharp viewer registers "this isn't a real photo of a real person" without being able to say why. On a platform where the photo's entire job is to make you feel authentic, that backfires badly. And there's a second problem that comes up constantly: the tools quietly shave a decade off you, slim your face, or smooth you into a person who doesn't quite match the one who walks into the interview. So the practical test is simple. If the generated photo still clearly looks like the current, actual you, use it. The moment it starts looking like a smoother, younger, glossier stranger, throw it out, because you're going to be met in person or on a video call, and the gap between the photo and the human is a worse first impression than an ordinary phone shot ever would have been. A slightly imperfect real photo beats a flawless fake one. The photo doesn't work alone A great photo gets you noticed, but noticing is only the first step. What happens next is the recruiter's eye slides right to your headline and the top of your profile, so the photo buys you a moment of attention that the rest of the profile has to earn. If the picture is sharp and the headline underneath it is a vague job title with no substance, you've spent your first impression and gotten nothing back. This is also why the visual and the words have to feel like the same person. A recent, human photo next to an About section that reads like it was pasted straight out of a chatbot creates a jarring mismatch, and that mismatch is its own quiet penalty. There's a growing recruiter allergy to AI-generated profile text for the same reason a fake-looking headshot backfires: both break the sense that a specific human is on the other end. The photo and the writing are a package. Fix the photo first because it's fast, then run through a broader LinkedIn profile optimization pass so the profile it sits on top of is worth the click it just earned. The honest question: when to remove your photo entirely Here's where the standard advice goes quiet, and where you deserve the real version. A photo doesn't just show your face. It reveals your approximate age, your race, your gender, and how conventionally attractive a stranger might find you. Every one of those is a trait a person could be biased about, consciously or not, and a photo hands all of it over before a recruiter has read a word about what you can do. That's not paranoia. Age bias in particular is real and well documented, and plenty of experienced job seekers can describe the moment a recruiter's face changes when the person who walks in is older than the photo implied, or older than they'd hoped. It's worth separating the real risk from the panic, though, because a lot of what people believe about how recruiters screen turns out to be myth rather than mechanism . For someone who has felt bias land repeatedly, the calculation is genuinely different. A photo that lifts replies on average may not be lifting yours, if it's the thing triggering a filter you'll never see. So the "remove it" question is a genuine judgment call, not a rule, and it cuts both ways. On the one side, a photo humanizes you, builds trust, and demonstrably gets more people to look and reply. On the other, it's a bias surface you don't strictly need, since neither US resumes nor LinkedIn actually require one. Most people, most of the time, are better off with a good photo up, because the reply-lift and the trust are worth more than the risk. But if you're over fifty, or you belong to a group that faces obvious hiring bias, and you've watched your response rate stay flat while your qualifications say it shouldn't, removing or minimizing the photo is a legitimate experiment, not a cop-out. You can even test it: run a few weeks with a photo, a few without, and watch what your inbound actually does. One nuance. Removing the photo works differently from having a bad one. A blank professional-looking profile that's otherwise complete reads as a deliberate choice. A profile that's missing a photo and half-finished reads as abandoned. If you go photo-less, make the rest of the profile airtight so the absence looks intentional. Country norms, and why your resume is a different story A lot of the confusion here comes from mixing up two different documents. The rules for a photo on a resume or CV and the rules for a photo on LinkedIn are not the same, and they vary by country on top of that. In the United States, the standard advice is to keep your photo off your resume entirely. It's partly a bias concern, tied to guidance that a photo can hand an employer knowledge of your race, gender, or age and become a liability in any later discrimination claim, so many recruiters simply set photo resumes aside. It's partly mechanical, because the software that parses resumes handles text, not images, and a photo can garble the parse. If you want to see the full case for keeping your face off the page, we walk through whether to put a picture on your resume separately. The short version for a US job search: photo off the resume. Other countries run the opposite convention. Germany is the classic example. A Lebenslauf without a photo has long been read as incomplete there, even though the country's equal-treatment law made application photos legally optional back in 2006. The rule changed; the habit didn't. Much of continental Europe, South Asia, and parts of East Asia expect a photo on the CV too. So a resume photo is a regional norm, not a universal one, and the safe move is to follow the convention of the country you're actually applying in. LinkedIn sits outside all of that. It's a single global professional network, and on LinkedIn a photo is the norm no matter where you live or what your local resume convention says. So the clean way to hold both facts at once: in the US, keep the photo off the resume and put your energy into a strong LinkedIn photo, which is where that face actually earns its keep. How often should you update your photo? Not on a schedule. Before it stops looking like you. The test is one question: if a connection met you for coffee tomorrow, would they recognize you from the profile without a beat of confusion? A photo drifts out of date when your hair, your weight, your glasses, or just the accumulated years have moved on far enough that the picture and the person stop matching. The specific trap to avoid is reverting to a younger, better version of yourself after a setback like a layoff. It's an understandable impulse and it almost always reads wrong, because the gap surfaces the instant you meet anyone, and it signals the exact anxiety it's trying to hide. A current photo of who you are now, taken with care, does more for you than a flattering photo of who you were five years ago. Recognizable and recent beats impressive and stale. The pre-post checklist Before you save that photo, run it against this. It takes thirty seconds and catches almost everything. Can a stranger see your face clearly at thumbnail size, not only at full screen? Is it just you in the frame, with no cropped-out arms or second faces? Are your eyes visible, meaning no sunglasses and no hat brim in the way? Do you look approachable, a real slight smile rather than a stony stare or a forced grin? Is the light soft and even, with no harsh shadow across your face? Is the background plain and quiet? Are you dressed about a notch above the role you want? Does the photo look like you right now, not you from several years and one hairstyle ago? Is it a real photo, not a logo, cartoon, or an AI render that's drifted away from your actual face? If you can answer yes down the line, upload it. You've just fixed the highest-return, lowest-effort thing on your entire profile, and you did it in about the time it takes to make coffee. Frequently Asked Questions Does a LinkedIn photo really get you more recruiter replies? Yes. Be skeptical of the exact multipliers, though. Those "profiles with a photo get many times the views" figures are old, LinkedIn-attributed, and hard to pin to a live source, so treat them as folklore, not math. What holds up is the direction, and it is not really in dispute: a clear, friendly face gets noticed and answered more than a blank grey circle. A recruiter scanning a wall of thumbnails wants a real person to contact. Be one. Is a blank profile better than a bad photo? Usually the bad photo still wins, as long as your face is clear and you look presentable, because a missing photo reads as an incomplete or abandoned account. There's one exception. A cartoon, a company logo, or a heavily filtered render can actually be worse than the blank grey default, since those fight the trust a real face is supposed to build. In doubt, an ordinary clear photo of you beats both. Can I use a selfie? A well-taken one, sure. Nobody's demanding a studio session. What recruiters can't stand is the obvious car selfie with the seatbelt slashing across your chest, or the bathroom-mirror shot with the toilet in frame. Move to a plain wall near a window, hand the phone to a friend so it's taken from a couple of feet back, and the same phone produces something that reads as a real portrait instead of a grabbed one. Do I need to pay a professional photographer? No. Skip the invoice. A phone in portrait mode, window light or open shade, a plain wall, a solid top, and a friend to hit the shutter gets you most of the way in about ten minutes. Pro headshots are a nice-to-have that plenty of well-regarded people never bothered with. The recruiter is not grading production value. They want a clear, well-lit, approachable face, and a phone delivers that fine. Are AI headshot generators a good idea? They can work. One real caveat, though. Some AI headshots land in an uncanny zone that a sharp viewer clocks as not-quite-real, which quietly undoes the authenticity the photo was supposed to buy, and the tools love to shave years and pounds off you. Use one only if the output still clearly looks like the current, actual you. You'll be met in person or on video eventually, and a glossy fake that doesn't match the human is a worse first impression than a plain phone shot ever was. Should I smile in my LinkedIn photo? A real, slight smile is the sweet spot. A stern closed-mouth stare makes you look guarded, and a giant forced grin looks staged, so you want the middle. Picture the expression you'd wear greeting someone you're genuinely glad to see, and look right into the lens so the photo feels like eye contact with whoever's viewing it. That warmth is part of the same signal you're sending when you build a personal brand on LinkedIn . Should I put a photo on my resume too? In the US, no. Keep it off. Recruiters often set photo resumes aside over bias concerns, and the software that parses your resume reads text, not images, so a photo can garble the whole parse. Your photo belongs on LinkedIn instead. Germany and much of Europe and Asia are the exception, since a CV photo is expected there, so match the country you're applying in. Is it a good idea to remove my photo to avoid bias? It's a legitimate judgment call, not a rule, and it depends on you. A photo humanizes you and lifts replies for most people, so most people should keep a good one up. But a photo also reveals your age, race, and gender, which is a bias surface you don't strictly need. If you face obvious hiring bias and your response rate stays flat despite strong qualifications, removing or minimizing the photo is a fair experiment. If you go photo-less, make the rest of the profile airtight so the absence looks deliberate. How often should I update my LinkedIn photo? Not on a fixed schedule. Update it when it stops looking like you. If a connection would hesitate to recognize you at a coffee meeting, you're overdue. The move to avoid is reverting to a younger, better version of yourself after a layoff, because the gap surfaces the second you meet anyone and reads as exactly the insecurity it's trying to cover. Recent and recognizable wins. What background works best? Something plain and quiet. A blank wall, a clean office, a softly blurred outdoor scene, anything that doesn't compete with your face. Skip the vacation backdrop, the neon sign, the crowded party crop. And if the only photo you love has a messy background behind it, free removal tools will swap in a plain color in about a minute, and your face still carries the shot. title: Why Solo Division 8 Estimators Turn Away Winnable Bids
summary: A solo Division 8 estimator turns away winnable bids every week, usually small dense jobs and poorly drawn sets. See what actually changes the takeoff math.
body_text: It’s 4:30 on a Thursday. Two sets of plans are sitting unopened in your inbox, the bid you’re already on isn’t finished, and both of those jobs will walk before Monday. There’s one of you, and there’s only so much Thursday. Every solo Division 8 estimator runs the same quiet math. You take the jobs you can finish. You pass on the ones you can’t get to. The ones you pass on don’t register as lost work, because the day is already full when you make the call. They register as triage. Triage has a cost, though, and for a solo Division 8 estimator that cost is real money leaving the building every week. You do the takeoff, write the estimate, and manage the job once it’s won, all off one desk. When a fresh set of plans lands and you’re already three deep, something gives. Usually it’s the newest job. Sometimes it’s the hardest one. It’s almost never the one that wasn’t worth winning. Which Jobs a Solo Estimator Actually Walks Away From Ask a solo Division 8 estimator which bids they skip and the answer catches people off guard. It isn’t the hospital with four thousand openings. It’s the small stuff. “Usually the jobs we turn away are the smaller ones,” one solo estimator in the Southwest said. “Smaller ones have more work per door leaf basically.” That line carries the whole insight. A 30-opening job isn’t a shrunk-down version of a 300-opening job. Per leaf, it’s often denser. You still read the full spec. You still match hardware sets to openings. You still chase the same coordination between the door schedule, the floor plans, and the hardware spec. There are just fewer doors to spread that work across, so the hours per leaf climb. The labor-to-revenue ratio tilts against you on the small ones. So they sit. Then there’s the second pile. High-dollar jobs skipped because the drawings are a mess. “Some of the ones we turn away would be high-dollar ones that are just difficult or they’re poorly drawn or whatever else.” Good money left on the table, because a bad set carries an unpredictable time cost, and unpredictable time is the one thing a one-person shop can’t absorb. A messy job might take four hours to take off, or fourteen. You can’t schedule around a number you don’t have. It’s the same dynamic that makes bids scatter on incomplete drawings: nobody’s pricing quite the same scope. A solo estimator can price a hard job. What stops them is a job whose hours they can’t predict before they commit to it. The Bandwidth Math Nobody Writes Down For a one-person shop, every hour carries an opportunity cost, and the opportunity cost is another bid. An hour spent untangling a contradictory 30-door set is an hour not spent on a clean 200-door job you’d have won. The math never lands on paper, but it runs in the background of every bid-or-no-bid call you make. The limit on a solo Division 8 shop is throughput. One person, reading one set at a time, can only move so fast, and effort doesn’t raise the ceiling. A second estimator would, but most solo shops can’t justify the hire until the work is steady, and the work won’t get steady while winnable bids keep walking. That’s the loop. What Changes Throughput for a Solo Division 8 Estimator This is where AI takeoff earns its place, if it earns it at all. For a solo estimator, the value is personal reach: one person covering the ground a small team used to. Fresco, an AI takeoff tool built only for Division 8 doors, frames, and hardware, puts that reach in the estimator’s own scale. As Fresco’s team put it to one solo estimator during a demo, taking off a project of about 400 openings would take less time than that estimator currently spends on a 30-opening job by hand. That speed comes from removing the parts of the takeoff that eat the most time on a messy set. Fresco reads the full drawing set at once and flags the contradictions a manual takeoff has to hunt for. A door that shows up on the schedule but not the floor plans. A door on the plans that never made the schedule. One solo estimator watched both surface on his own project within minutes: “The architect has exactly those two problems for us.” Those are the same document contradictions we broke down in the fake door schedule problem. It also handles the counting traps that quietly cost jobs. A door that appears across a match line, showing up in section A and again in section C when it’s really one opening, gets deduplicated automatically instead of double-counted. Fresco’s own origin story is a shop that missed 200 doors on a job in Denver and lost the job because of it. You Still Sign the Bid None of this takes your name off the number. The estimator still owns the bid, and that matters more to a solo operator than to anyone, because when you’re the whole shop, there’s no one to catch your miss and no one to split the blame. It’s the accountability reality every estimator names about AI takeoffs, and it’s worth reading in full in why most estimators don’t trust AI takeoffs. The tool compresses the production work and leaves the judgment with you. When a solo estimator stress-tests it, and they always do, they check the things that actually bite. Multiple layers of sheetrock changing a frame’s throat depth. A door called hollow metal on the schedule and drawn as storefront aluminum on the elevation. Fresco flags the conflict. You make the call. And the record of every one of those calls stays with the takeoff, so when a GC challenges your number, you can show what you found and how you resolved it. The judgment on a Division 8 bid still belongs to the estimator. What AI takeoff removes is the mechanical work underneath it. When This Won’t Solve Your Problem The throughput argument only matters if throughput is your constraint. If you’ve already got the capacity to bid everything that comes in, faster takeoffs won’t move your win rate. Buy for a different reason, or don’t buy. There’s also the handoff question. A lot of solo shops run their takeoff and their project management through one tool, often Protek, so the estimate becomes the PM baseline the moment the job is won. Fresco has native paths into Comsense and eMullion. It doesn’t have one into Protek yet, so that back-feed is a manual Excel export today. If your whole workflow depends on that data moving without a manual step, factor the friction in before you switch. Frequently Asked Questions Can one person really run Division 8 takeoffs with AI, or do you need a team? One person can. An AI takeoff tool built for Division 8 gives a solo estimator the reach of a small team without the headcount. It reads the full set, matches hardware, and flags discrepancies in the time a manual takeoff spends on the first few sheets, then hands the review back to you. The bottleneck a second hire would solve, raw takeoff hours, is the one the software removes. Will AI takeoff work on poorly drawn plans, or only clean sets? Poorly drawn sets are where it earns its keep. The contradictions that make a set painful by hand, doors that don’t match between the schedule and the plans, hardware that conflicts across documents, are exactly what a Division 8 AI is built to catch. The messier the drawings, the more it saves you. Do I still control the final numbers if the software does the takeoff? Yes. The estimator owns the bid start to finish. The software produces the takeoff and flags every discrepancy; you decide what to do with each one. The record of those calls stays attached to the takeoff for when a GC questions the number later. Does Fresco work with Comsense, eMullion, or Protek? Fresco has native integrations with Comsense and eMullion, so a finished takeoff moves into either without re-entering data. It doesn’t integrate with Protek yet. Protek users can still move the takeoff over through an Excel export, but that’s a manual step rather than a one-click handoff. Are small door jobs even worth bidding? Often, yes, and they get skipped for the wrong reason. Small Division 8 jobs carry more work per door leaf, so they feel inefficient, but that density is a takeoff-speed problem, not a margin problem. When the takeoff stops eating the hours, the small jobs a solo shop used to turn away start penciling out. Fresco is an AI takeoff tool built only for Division 8 doors, frames, and hardware, made for estimators who need to bid more without hiring. See how it handles your plans at fresco.build.

title: Vertiv Hosts Latin American Partner Summit
summary: Vertiv held its first Latin America Partner Summit in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, March 19 - 22. Presented by Vertiv’s regional senior management team, channel partners received a firsthand view of Vertiv’s channel and product strategy for 2019.
body_text: Blog Posts Vertiv recognizes outstanding major channel partners and shares the company’s business and solution strategy for the region Sunrise, FL [March 25, 2019] – Vertiv held its first Latin America Partner Summit in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, March 19 - 22. Presented by Vertiv’s regional senior management team, channel partners received a firsthand view of Vertiv’s channel and product strategy for 2019. Additionally, the Vertiv Partner Program was unveiled, designed to maximize their success through their partnership with Vertiv. “We are pleased that our partners were able to join us during our first partner summit for the Latin America region, as they are an integral part of helping us deliver innovative, holistic solutions and expert support as the lines between traditional IT and telecom become blurred at the edge and in data centers of all sizes,” said Ricardo Duque, vice president of channel strategy for Vertiv Americas. “We are confident that our robust Vertiv Partner program will contribute to the success of our partners so that we can together meet our customers’ needs while achieving our business goals.” The Vertiv Latin America Partner Summit presented the opportunity to recognize the highest performing partners of 2018. The winning companies were selected based on their commitment to promoting the vital applications of the digital world and supporting today’s cutting-edge computer, mobile and cloud markets with Vertiv IT infrastructure solutions. Outstanding partners were recognized in six categories: Business Growth : The largest continuous growth in sales over the past year. Awarded to Grupo UPS S.A., Panama. Best Strategic Project: A project that reflects success for the client, high visibility to Vertiv and an additional source of business over the short term. Awarded to Vecodata S.A.C., Peru. Best Innovation: A partner or a project that has demonstrated the use of an innovative approach to position and sell Vertiv solutions in a highly competitive and complex environment. Awarded to Servicios Globales de Informática IT, Argentina. Best Network Edge Solution: A partner or project that kept the Vertiv promise to be the most effective company providing edge solutions to clients. Awarded to Sertres del Norte , Mexico. Best Energy Efficiency Solution : A partner or project that had a positive impact on energy savings or which had a positive impact on the environment. Awarded to Union , Brazil.
